CONTEXT HANDOFF — bolt-v2 conditional-fallback investigation (2026-07-08)

INTENT (read this first)
The owner's #1 standing concern in this repo is conditional fallbacks: code that,
when an input/config/file is missing or malformed, silently substitutes something
and continues instead of failing loudly. Multiple sessions have attacked instances
of this (verifier gates, poison locks, typed defaults) and each sweep was declared
"the real fix" — yet fallbacks KEEP APPEARING, including in brand-new PRs. The owner
believes prior sessions (including the one writing this handoff) have not understood
the phenomenon END-TO-END: something structural that we own keeps GENERATING
fallbacks downstream. Your mission is to build that end-to-end understanding from
primary evidence, then bring the owner a root-cause diagnosis and a class-level
execution plan. Understanding comes first; do not start fixing sites.

THE ENTRY-POINT EXAMPLE (owner-supplied, NOT yet examined — start here)
https://github.com/seungpyoson/bolt-v2/pull/1297/commits
Commit 1 is a straightforward config-value change. Commit 2 then adds many
conditional fallbacks. The owner asks: WHY does a simple value edit force a second
commit full of tolerance code? Reconstruct the causal chain precisely: read both
commit diffs, the PR conversation, and the CI runs between the commits
  verifier family: ~240 except-then-return/pass/continue candidates; 60 " or {}/
  []/()" substitutions (only 23 inside the swept verify_* family); 32
  "if not X.exists()" branches outside verify_*. These are CANDIDATES, not
  confirmed debt — past audits show many are legitimately fail-closed (returning
  a finding is loud) or legitimately optional. Blind conversion is dangerous
  (a prior blanket-panic attempt would have bricked order admission — PR #1141).

WHAT IS ALREADY DONE (do not redo; verify anchors if you rely on them)
- PR #1286 (merged 07-07): verifier discovery floors fail closed via
  verifier_io.require_nonempty + an AST-census meta-fence (test_verifier_io.py)
  that pins every call site. This is the accepted class-closure pattern here.
- PR #1281 (merged 07-07): sealed FinancialValue trait; Default on money types
  is now a compile error; Python fence with closed-world line allowlists.
- Poison-lock class extinct in production Rust.
- Confirmed-open micro-items: F-N1 (naming-audit rows with typo'd/missing
  from/to keys silently unenforced — two-arm repro exists, see memory
  project_pr1286_review), pilot-verifier floors, dual-TOML-parser fallback in
  scripts/rust_verification.py (parse_minimal_toml when _toml is None; 3 sites).
- OPEN epic items: #1070 F2 (fail-direction adjudication of ALL conditional
  fallbacks) and #1071 F1 (permanent fence). Your work IS the front end of F2.

UNVERIFIED HYPOTHESES about the generator (from the prior session; the owner has
NOT endorsed these — test them against the PR evidence, discard freely):
(a) No shared strict config-loading seam: each of 174 scripts hand-rolls config
    reading, so every new/changed key breeds local .get(default)/or-{} tolerance.
(b) Gates and test fixtures make tolerance cheaper than correctness: partial
    fixtures force production code to tolerate absence to go green; "optional
    strict config section" patterns have merged as recently as this week.
(c) Migration reflex: "if new key present use it, else old behavior" bridges
    that never get removed.
The owner's own framing: "something that we have just results in these" — find
the actual something(s). It may be none of the above.

BINDING OWNER RULES for whatever you propose
- No conditional fallbacks: silent substitute-and-continue is banned; loud
  hold/defer/halt is fine. Fail-direction must be adjudicated per site, not
  blanket-converted.
- Fix the class at the boundary, not the leaves; a plan that is 330 point-edits
  is wrong by construction. Equally: "add a validation layer" is not a fix if
  the generating behavior stays — fences are accepted only as the enforcement
  half of a real behavior fix (the #1286/#1281 precedent).
- Understand before coding; plan first and get owner approval; Codex implements
  (you write briefs), Claude owns design/triage/review.
- Evidence discipline: every claim needs a personally-reproducible anchor
  (file:symbol at your HEAD, command output you ran). Differential tests must
  be shown to fail on the buggy code. Anchor briefs on symbols, not line numbers.
- Process: GitHub Issues first (search before creating; ONE consolidated issue,
  not one per finding), branch-first, no close-keywords anywhere ("Part of #N").
  CI is python3.12. No manual full-CI dispatches. Outward GitHub actions
  (comments, issues) need explicit per-target owner approval.
- Owner is non-technical: plain English, short replies, lead with recommendation.
  Never declare merge-ready; report state + evidence.

PERSISTENT MEMORY (full context lives here; the index is auto-loaded)
~/.agent/projects/-Users-spson-Projects-Claude-bolt-v2/memory/MEMORY.md
Key files: project_1068_techdebt_epic (campaign state + 15-step blueprint),
project_pr1286_review / project_pr1281_review (post-merge findings incl. F-N1),
feedback_no_conditional_fallbacks, feedback_no_gates_as_fixes,
feedback_class_closure_boundary_not_leaf, feedback_verify_before_claim.

PARALLEL LANES (do not collide, do not conflate)
- PRICE P1 (typed-money step 7, Rust core) — brief ready, may launch separately.
- Micro-PR (F-N1 + pilot floors + dual-TOML) — pending owner authorization.
- Your investigation is Python-side and collision-free with both.

DELIVERABLE, IN ORDER
1. The #1297 causal chain, precisely reconstructed, plus confirming/refuting
   examples: what pressure manufactures fallback commits.
2. Root-cause diagnosis of the generator(s), evidence-anchored.
3. A class-level execution plan: the boundary fix that removes the generating
   pressure, the adjudicated sweep of existing sites (classified fail-closed /
   legitimate / real-debt, with generator attribution), and the fence that makes
   regrowth structurally impossible — with sizes, sequencing, collision analysis,
   and the owner-decision points listed explicitly.
Stop for owner approval after (3). Do not implement anything before that.

One note: the prompt deliberately marks my generator hypotheses as unverified and tells the new session to start from #1297 — the example you pointed at that I never actually examined — so it builds the understanding you're saying is missing rather than inheriting my framing.

I'm picking up the conditional-fallback investigation. Starting with the entry-point example: PR #1297 — I'll reconstruct why a simple config change forced a second commit full of tolerance code. First, the repo entrypoint and the PR itself.

1	# bolt-v2 Agent Rules
2	
3	Repo governance for agents; higher-level standing instructions apply.
4	
5	## Precedence & Source Of Truth
6	
7	- Direct user instructions win unless they violate safety.
8	- `AGENTS.md` is the governance source and operational entrypoint. `CLAUDE.md`, `GEMINI.md`, SpecKit prompts, Superpowers skills, and plugin docs are adapters — if they conflict, follow `AGENTS.md` and report the drift.
9	- `.specify/memory/constitution.md` records SpecKit principles; update it only when governance changes those principles or gates. The active SpecKit plan is feature context, not governance.
10	- After a merge, `main` is authoritative; old branches, worktrees, and plan pointers become reference-only immediately after supersession or merge. Do not continue from stale work or cite it as proof that accepted scope is missing from `main`; port only proven-missing scope onto a fresh branch from `main`.
11	
12	## Agent & Plugin Discipline
13	
14	- Do not create per-agent policy docs unless the tool loads them and the policy cannot live in `AGENTS.md`. For tools that do not load it, pass `AGENTS.md` as read-only context; add `.specify/memory/constitution.md` only when SpecKit principles or gates matter.
15	- `ci/ai-review.toml` is the machine-readable AI-review mirror authority for PR-Agent, which cannot load arbitrary repo files in GitHub Actions; `scripts/verify_ai_review_governance.py` checks `.pr_agent.toml` against that config in CI.
16	- AI review deliverables must identify the reviewer source and exact configured model. Runtime source/model labels and comment markers come from `ci/ai-review.toml`; workflow and prompt text must not embed those runtime values.
17	- Do not patch plugin caches as durable fixes; use repo governance, SpecKit templates, verified extension/override surfaces, or regenerated adapters. Generated prompts may recommend strict TDD — use Evidence-Driven Verification unless the user, active spec, or risk requires TDD.
18	
19	## Scope Discipline
20	
21	- One branch or PR may cover only one declared issue, spec, task, or an explicitly named slice of one broader item; slice PRs and their review requests must name remaining accepted scope and where it is tracked.
22	- Reviewers must flag out-of-scope changes, hidden adjacent issue work, and missing claimed scope as findings. Do not claim a PR closes a broader issue unless the diff actually satisfies it.
23	
24	## Repo Rules
25	
26	1. **NO HARDCODES** — every runtime value comes from TOML config. No string literals for IDs, quantities, timeouts, or any runtime value in code.
27	2. **NO DUAL PATHS** — one way to do each thing: one config format, one secret source, one build path.
28	3. **NO DEBTS** — no TODO, no "fix later", no unpinned dependencies, no uncommitted work.
29	4. **NO CREDENTIAL DISPLAY** — never cat/print/log API keys, private keys, secrets.
30	5. **PURE RUST BINARY** — standalone Rust `LiveNode` using NT's Rust API directly. No Python layer, PyO3, maturin, or pip.
31	6. **SSM IS THE SINGLE SECRET SOURCE** — product/runtime credentials resolve from AWS SSM via `aws-sdk-ssm`. No AWS CLI subprocess, no 1Password CLI, no environment variable fallbacks, no other secret backends. GitHub Actions repository automation may use GitHub's ephemeral `GITHUB_TOKEN` only for GitHub API operations; do not add alternate GitHub token names. `JULES_API_KEY` may live in GitHub Actions secrets only for repository code-maintenance advisory workflows; it is not a product/runtime/deploy/live/trading secret, not an alternate GitHub token, and must not be exposed to AWS, market data, order execution, runtime, deploy, or live jobs.
32	7. **GROUP BY CHANGE** — values that share a lifecycle live in one config section; a wallet, credential-set, or venue swap must require one edit.
33	8. **DO NOT REFERENCE BOLT V1** — do not read, import, or depend on `~/Projects/Claude/bolt/`. NT source is in `~/.cargo/git/checkouts/nautilus_trader-*/` or GitHub.
34	9. **STRATEGIES PRODUCE INTENT ONLY** — strategies emit order intent and strategy-local signal state only. Admissibility, venue rules, fillability, rounding, minimum size, fee-adjusted sizing, and submit gating live in shared NT-based execution/admission modules. Submit mechanics under `src/strategies/*` are rejected unless explicitly approved as strategy-local signal logic.
35	10. **CHAINLINK DATA STREAMS: TESTNET IS PRODUCTION** — for the `price_to_beat` oracle, testnet is the only final environment because mainnet credentials cannot be obtained. Treat the testnet Chainlink stream as production for this oracle; do not raise testnet-vs-mainnet as a concern or ask for reconfirmation solely because the stream is testnet. Still verify config-schema compatibility, service health, fail-closed behavior, and exact-head verification.
36	11. **PROVIDER/RUNTIME BOUNDARY EVIDENCE IS REGISTERED** — every deploy/readiness feeder that depends on provider runtime bytes or metadata must be represented in the authoritative boundary registry and guarded by source-fence evidence or an issue-bound, expiring non-WebSocket deferral. WebSocket-frame evidence must not be deferred.
37	
38	## Evidence-Driven Verification
39	
40	- TDD is allowed but not mandatory unless the user, active spec, or risk requires it; `.specify/memory/constitution.md` mirrors this principle.
41	- Agents do not wait on CI: push, report the head SHA, detach — verifying results at head belongs to the reviewer.
42	- Every claim must map to evidence: tests, static checks, source-fence results, remote CI, live artifacts, direct inspection, or explicit user-approved risk acceptance that does not violate a MUST rule. Every plan or task list must name the evidence for each changed requirement or risk: production behavior needs behavior/integration/remote-CI/live artifacts (or user-approved risk acceptance that does not violate a MUST rule); trading, admission, secrets, and config also need fail-closed evidence for invalid or missing inputs plus exact-head proof before any live operation; refactors need existing tests/static checks/source-fence or documented structural-equivalence review proving behavior is unchanged; documentation, prompt, template, and policy changes require targeted text/static checks plus internal adversarial review before completion claims.
43	- External review: only after local findings are resolved and exact-head CI or the user-approved equivalent is green.
44	
45	## Remote-First Rust Verification
46	
47	- Do not run local compile-heavy Rust verification by default: no managed `just` Rust test/build/clippy recipes, no raw cargo refused by `ci/rust-verification.toml` `[local_compile_policy]`. Use local non-compile gates for fast feedback: `just fmt-check`, `just deny`, `just ci-lint-workflow`, Python verifiers, and `just source-fence-static` (public recipes only, never `*-inner`).
48	- Default to draft PRs while iterating; for Rust feedback, commit, publish with `just sandbox-safe-push`, open a draft PR, then run `just verify-remote` for exact-head Ubicloud/GitHub Actions. `just sandbox-safe-push` is the sandboxed branch-publishing path because it pushes by the configured remote URL and verifies exact remote HEAD without writing local upstream or remote-tracking metadata. Do not embed credentials in Git push URLs; use credential helpers or SSH agent auth so credentials are not exposed through process arguments. Do not use raw remote-name pushes such as `git push origin ...` from a managed sandbox; if one is used accidentally and Git prints a local ref-update warning after the remote push, verify the exact remote head and continue with `just sandbox-safe-push`. Draft pushes defer full-CI merge proof (clippy/deny still run) and cannot merge. For merge proof, mark the PR ready and run `just verify-remote` for the required exact-head PR gate, or use the merge queue gate (see [Operator Policy](docs/ci/ubicloud-cost-governance.md#operator-policy)). Operator break-glass is for exceptional local repro and live/operator lanes only, never a normal agent path.
49	- Queue through `just merge-queue <pr...>`, not by commenting the Mergify command directly. The recipe resolves exact remote SHAs, runs merge-queue preflight once, and posts the configured queue command only for a `queue_as_one_wave` verdict.
50	- Cooperative paths are gated through `just`, `scripts/rust_verification.py`, `.no-mistakes.yaml`, and the PATH cargo shim (`scripts/cargo-shim`, `scripts/install-cargo-shim`), which reads `[local_compile_policy]`. Lanes self-serialize via `[local_lane_policy]`: verifier entry points and broad gates acquire the lane through `scripts/local_verification_gate.py` (broad gates once, competing gates fail fast), CI (`allowed_ci_env`) bypasses the lock, and coverage drift fails `source-fence-static` via `scripts/verify_lane_governance.py`. Known bypasses: absolute-path cargo, `rustup run ... cargo`, cross-repo cargo, old daemons, non-shim PATHs, startup-skipping shells, direct `rustc`.
51	
52	## Rust Probe Policy
53	
54	- Ready-PR or merge-queue full CI is proof; draft `workflow_dispatch` full CI is feedback; Rust Probe is debugging — use it only when cheap local checks cannot answer the question, and never to replace the required `gate`.
55	- Run `just rust-probe suggest` first; dispatch `just rust-probe ...` only from a clean named branch whose pushed `HEAD` SHA is used (dispatch refuses unsafe local state). Before dispatch, state changed files, suspected failure class, mode, target, and smallest-sufficient rationale. Limits: max 2 probe runs before stopping to explain root cause; full CI may run only after the slice is coherent; Rust Probe success is not merge readiness; do not run full CI just to discover ordinary compiler errors.
56	- Suggested integration-test probes use the Cargo `[[test]]` harness as `test_target`; when a changed file is a harness member module, the suggested `test_name` is `<member_stem>::` so nextest stays scoped to that module.
57	
58	## Review Bar & Merge Mechanics
59	
60	- Every unique substantive issue is a finding regardless of severity; do not downgrade real issues into notes or treat tracked as resolved unless fixed or explicitly waived.
61	- Before completing or merging coding work, open a PR and request review from the GitHub account with node ID `U_kgDOEZMFhA` (login-based — resolve the node ID to its current login and keep `.github/CODEOWNERS` aligned). This required-reviewer node ID is an intentional hardcoded policy constant for native merge governance: PR-editable config must not select the required reviewer.
62	- The `main` ruleset must require native code-owner review, stale-review dismissal, last-push approval, and review-thread resolution; if those are missing, stop and report the blocker instead of treating CI checks as merge controls. Agents must not merge, squash, rebase-merge, or otherwise land code until the PR has approval from node ID `U_kgDOEZMFhA`; if review cannot be requested, stop and report.
63	- Do not request external review with uncommitted changes, unpushed commits, unresolved findings, unanswered comments, or non-green exact-head CI. Reply to and resolve every applicable review thread (give the technical reason for any inapplicable one); commit and push any remaining fix before further review discussion.
64	- Verify each active `main` rule before merge: list with `gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/rules/branches/main`, confirm checks green in `gh pr view <n> --json statusCheckRollup` and approvals met. On a stale block, force recompute by push, review, close/reopen, or waiting; never force past a green-but-cached block with `gh pr merge --admin`.
65	
66	## Response Format
67	
68	- Keep responses concise by default; prefer short direct answers over long explanations unless depth is requested.
69

# tech-debt: consolidate verify_ci_workflow_hygiene.py from literal substring checks to structural/semantic invariants
## Problem
`scripts/verify_ci_workflow_hygiene.py` (10,872 lines) + `scripts/test_verify_ci_workflow_hygiene.py` (10,525 lines) enforce `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (and a couple of sibling workflows) almost entirely by asserting that hundreds of exact text fragments are present (`if FRAGMENT not in archive_text: errors.append(...)`). Consequences:

- **Duplicated source of truth** — the verifier is close to a transcription of `ci.yml` re-expressed as assertions; the workflow and the verifier must change in lockstep (violates the repo's single-source-of-truth rule).
- **Brittle** — substring / `shlex` matching trips on benign reformatting; checks couple to incidental whitespace and ordering rather than intent.
- **Low signal-to-line ratio** — ~21k lines (rules + tests) to police one workflow, and it only grows (e.g., #1011 added ~18 more literal-check lines for the sccache fail-open contract).

## Expected Outcome
The CI-config contract is enforced by tens of **structural / semantic invariants** evaluated against a parsed model of the workflow(s) rather than literal-text presence — e.g. "gate depends on test-archive", "no job sets `RUSTC_WRAPPER` directly", "required jobs ⊆ runner-tier map", "sccache cache steps are non-fatal". Equal-or-stronger coverage at a fraction of the lines.

## Approach Notes
- Parse `ci.yml` once into a YAML-faithful model; assert invariants against the model. #879 already proposes exactly this for the merge_group concurrency slice — extend that approach file-wide instead of inventing a second mechanism.
- Migrate incrementally, invariant family by family, keeping the existing literal checks + tests as the regression net (differential parity before deleting any check).
- Keep genuinely-literal pins where the intent *is* the exact string (pinned action SHAs, "must not set `RUSTC_WRAPPER`").
- Non-goals: changing what CI does; weakening any guardrail; a big-bang rewrite.

## Risks
This is load-bearing security / governance infra (gate integrity, deploy-trust, hermeticity). A subtle regression could silently weaken a guardrail. High blast radius → migrate behind the existing tests with differential parity, never rewrite blind. Reversible per slice (revert a migrated family).

## Verification
- Per migrated family: prove the new structural check fails on the *same* mutations the old literal check caught (differential), and `python3 scripts/test_verify_ci_workflow_hygiene.py` + `just ci-lint-workflow` stay green at each step.
- Net line reduction plus retained mutation coverage is the done signal.

## Relations
Related to #879 (YAML-faithful parse for the merge_group concurrency slice — effectively the first slice of this), #906 (perf: same verifier re-computes work; parse-once helps), #333 (CI epic). Surfaced during #1011 (sccache wiring).

Interim status of what is already established from my own runs:

**The #1297 causal chain is fully reconstructed and reproduced:**
1. Commit 1 changed 2 values in `.mergify.yml`. CI went red because those exact literals are mirrored in three more places: the hygiene verifier's expectations (`verify_mergify_config` in `scripts/verify_ci_workflow_hygiene.py`), that verifier's own mutation tests (which hardcode both the config text and the expected error strings), and `MERGIFY_QUEUE_MAX_BATCH_SIZE` plus batch-split expectations in `scripts/test_merge_queue_preflight.py`. The failing job was `clippy` — whose "Setup environment" step runs the whole python governance battery, so the failure signal didn't even name the real cause.

Commit 2's oddest content — 21 new lines in the hand-rolled fallback TOML parser (`parse_minimal_toml`) — was forced by a **different, latent** breakage: PR #1255 (07-07) put a multiline array into `ci/rust-verification.toml`, which the fallback parser can't read. CI never noticed (its system python has `tomllib`); on every Mac, `/usr/bin/python3 -S scripts/rust_verification.py repo-status` has printed `invalid-policy` since then — I reproduced this on main, and confirmed the PR-head parser prints `managed`. - scripts/: 174 files, 168,783 lines — grew from 151,793 on 07-04 (+17k in 4 days, during the debt campaign). Growth curve: 2.2k (May 1) → 32.7k (Jun 1) → 146.5k (Jul 1) → 168.8k today.

## Config-value mirror topology — final findings

**Yes, #1297's "change 1 value → edit 4 files" is typical for anything in `.mergify.yml`, and a partial single-source mechanism already exists that the mergify path doesn't use.**

### Pinned values (value | config source | load-bearing mirror files)
| Value | Source | Mirror files (count) |
|---|---|---|
| batch_size default `max:10` (#1297) | .mergify.yml | **4** — verify_ci_workflow_hygiene.py (`rule_expectations`), test_verify_ci_workflow_hygiene.py, test_merge_queue_preflight.py (`MERGIFY_QUEUE_MAX_BATCH_SIZE`) |
| `batch_max_failure_resolution_attempts:0` (#1297) | .mergify.yml | **5** — verifier, its test, merge_queue_preflight.py, test_merge_queue_preflight.py |
| `checks_timeout:150 minutes` | .mergify.yml | **3** — verifier + its test |
| `approved-reviews-by = sp-reviewer` | .mergify.yml | **5** — verifier, its test, test_merge_queue_preflight.py, .github/CODEOWNERS |
| `check-success = backtester-gate` | .mergify.yml + backtester-ci.yml job | **~16** — MERGIFY_REQUIRED_MERGE_CONDITIONS, ci_provenance.py, coverage_enforcer.py, 4× ci/*.toml, 7+ tests |
| `check-success = host-health` | .mergify.yml + ci.yml job | **~15** |
| runner label `ubicloud-standard-4-arm` | ci/github-actions-runners.toml (single source) | **3** — actionlint.yaml, one test *(well-contained)* |
| rust toolchain `1.96.0` | rust-toolchain.toml | **3** — ci/developer-tool-storage-hygiene.toml, its test |
| `JUST_VERSION=1.49.0` | 8 workflow YAMLs | verifier enforces **parity**, not a literal → no verifier/test value mirror *(good pattern)* |

### Worst offenders
1. **CI gate/check names** (gate, backtester-gate, actionlint, host-health) — 15-16 files each; rarely change, so latent pain.
2. **Mergify structural scalars** (batch sizes, timeouts, reviewer, resolution-attempts) — 3-5 files each, and these actually change (that's #1297). The acute, recurring cost. All ~14 live as inline literals inside `verify_mergify_config` (verify_ci_workflow_hygiene.py:6560, 6813, 6837).

### Single-source mechanism? Yes — three patterns already in the repo:
- **`scripts/ci_provenance.py` is a real constants hub** (`POLICY_ROWS`, `GATE_NAME_KEYS`, `POLICY_REQUIRED_VALUES`, `REQUIRED_CHECK_INTEGRATION_ID`, `TARGET_REQUIRED_CHECK_CONTEXT`), imported by the hygiene verifier, coverage_enforcer, merge_readiness, verify_ci_path_filters. `merge_readiness.py` pulls gate names from `GATE_NAME_KEYS` instead of hardcoding — proof it works.
- **`ci/github-actions-runners.toml`** single-sources runner labels (workflows use `vars.*`); mirror footprint only 3 files.
- **Cross-file parity checks** (JUST_VERSION) instead of literal pins.

### Summary (compact)
The `.mergify.yml` governance surface is the outlier: `verify_mergify_config` inline-pins ~14 scalars, and both test suites restate the values *and* the mutated config text, so every value change cascades to 3-5 files — exactly the #1297 experience. The gate/check names are mirrored even wider (15-16 files) but change rarely. The rest of the repo already avoids this: runner labels, CI policy rows, and gate names are single-sourced through `ci_provenance.py` and `ci/github-actions-runners.toml`, and toolchain/JUST_VERSION use parity checks. The narrow, known fix is to hoist the mergify expectations into `ci_provenance.py` (or a new `mergify_policy` constants module) that the verifier, the preflight test, and the hygiene test import — collapsing the 3-5-file edit to 1, mirroring the pattern the repo already uses everywhere else.

# Why the governance layer manufactures code — diagnosis and redesign plan

**Root cause in one sentence:** the layer stores every fact about the repo in 3–6 places (the config itself, a verifier's hardcoded expectation, that verifier's hand-written test twin, and often a digest or allowlist), and CI demands all copies agree before anything goes green — so every ordinary change forces compensating commits, and the compensating style (more pins, more allowlists, more twins) is itself what gets written each time.

**Recommendation up front:** adopt one synthesized architecture — a rule-table kernel where each fact lives once and tests are *generated* from it (#1215 WS2 + #1016), sanctioned vocabulary modules replacing the 20k-line registry (#1275-17), one execution-context/IO seam replacing per-script tolerance code (F2 front end), with fences only as adoption-enforcement — sequenced in ~12–15 Codex sessions with golden-output safety at every step. Details and your decision points below. Nothing is implemented; this stops here for your approval.

## Part 1 — The mechanism, reconstructed from PR #1297 and five more PRs

**PR #1297** (open, currently green): commit 1 changed two numbers in `.mergify.yml` (batch max 10→6, failure-resolution attempts 0→3). CI went red — but not where you'd look: the failing job was `clippy`, because clippy's setup step runs the whole Python governance battery. Inside it, the hygiene verifier hardcodes the expected mergify values (`verify_mergify_config`), its test twin hardcodes both the config text and the exact error strings, and the preflight test hardcodes the batch size a third time. So a 2-line change required commit 2: +67/−16 across 4 more files just to make the copies agree.

Commit 2 also grew the hand-rolled backup TOML parser by 21 lines — and that part had nothing to do with mergify. On 07-07, PR #1255 put a multiline list into `ci/rust-verification.toml`. The backup parser (used when Python is too old for the real parser, i.e., on every Mac's system Python) can't read multiline lists. CI never noticed because CI's Python has the real parser. I reproduced it: on main, `/usr/bin/python3 -S scripts/rust_verification.py repo-status` prints `invalid-policy`; with #1297's fix it prints `managed`. The #1297 author's local gates tripped over this day-old latent breakage, so the fix rode into an unrelated mergify PR — unfiled, and passed by all three AI reviewers despite being out of scope. This is the second time this exact parser was grown this way (quoted-key support was chased in on 06-30, #1051).

**Five more merged PRs with the same shape** (from an 80-PR screen, 38 fully inspected; I personally re-verified the two worst):

- **#1151** (07-01): bump artifact retention to 14 days (~18 lines) → three follow-up commits, ~153 lines plus **two regenerations of binary test fixtures**, because provenance verifiers hash-pin the value across workflow, TOMLs, and fixture zips. Worst ratio: ~18:153.
- **#1107** (06-30): ~39-line fix to recognize ready Mergify proof PRs → red `gate`/`ci-policy` runs (reproduced from check-runs) → three follow-up commits, ~317 lines; the last commit is 100% test-twin, zero logic.
- **#1172** (07-02): remove a stale key from 4 workflows → two follow-up commits that touch **only** the giant verifier and its twin.
- **#1123** (06-30): add one new shared file → forced follow-up because a hand-maintained fingerprint registry doesn't auto-discover files.
- **#1186** (07-03): raise a build-jobs cap in one TOML (+12/−12) → +25 lines of test-fixture alignment.

The pressure that manufactures the second commit is always the same: a fence that stores its expectation as a **copy** rather than reading it from one shared home.

## Part 2 — Diagnosis: six properties of the layer that generate code (measured)

All numbers below are from commands I ran today at main `fb03ab8b1` unless attributed.

1. **Literal mirroring, no single source.** ~14 mergify scalars are inline literals in the verifier; each change cascades to 3–5 files; CI check names are mirrored in ~15–16 files. Measured lockstep tax: **67 of 78 commits touching ci.yml since 06-01 (86%) also had to edit the hygiene verifier.** The fix pattern already exists in-repo and works: `ci_provenance.py:53-80` is a constants hub imported by 7+ scripts; runner labels are single-sourced in `ci/github-actions-runners.toml` (3-file footprint); JUST_VERSION uses a parity check instead of value mirrors. The mergify surface is the un-migrated outlier.

2. **Hand-written test twins that restate each verifier.** `test_*.py` is **92,982 lines = 55% of the entire layer**. The giant pair (`verify_ci_workflow_hygiene.py` 16,506 + twin 19,133) is 35,639 lines to police ~15 workflow files, and the twin's ~369 mutation assertions are 53% of the 6.2-minute local battery (#1215 measurement). The #1215 audit found ~280 of those 369 are mechanically derivable from a rule table. #1172 and #1107 show entire commits that exist only to feed the twin.

3. **Content-addressed pins on cooperative surfaces.** Digest pins and exact line/count allowlists are the house pattern for *tamper* surfaces (correct — that's the #1220 lesson). But applied to cooperative config they turn routine edits into fixture regenerations: #1151's binary zip digests; #1281's money fence pinning *every* line in src/ containing "Default" (~28 count-sensitive entries — any future routine `#[derive(Default)]` edits the money fence); the runtime-literal registry now at **20,747 lines / 2,592 entries** (+150 entries in one week), already a known merge-conflict engine.

4. **Shadow implementations bred by degraded-context contracts.** Because enforcement scripts must run under macOS system Python 3.9 (no stdlib TOML parser), **three hand-rolled TOML parsers** exist (`rust_verification.py`, `cargo-shim`, `sandbox_safe_push.py`), each supporting a different dialect subset, with zero tests that compare them to the real parser — which is why #1255 silently broke the Mac lane for a day. The same pressure generalizes: the survey of new conditional fallbacks since 06-24 found the top driver is *sandbox/degraded-context tolerance* (e.g., `git_remote_utils.py:72-83` silently proceeds without auth when token env is absent; the code-review workflow swallows git errors twice and falls through; this week's one optional-config bridge, `smart_trigger`, defaults to *triggering*). Notably: the verifier/fence family itself held fail-closed discipline this window — #1286's floors work; the fallback frontier has moved to operational scripts.

5. **Latent breakage lands wherever it's discovered.** Green-before-push plus no-debts means whoever trips a latent cross-lane break fixes it inside their unrelated PR (#1297 commit 2), with no issue filed and no class review — so the shadow implementations quietly grow instead of getting questioned.

6. **The layer grows faster than the campaign shrinks it.** scripts/ went **2.2k lines (May 1) → 32.7k (Jun 1) → 56.7k (Jun 15) → 146.5k (Jul 1) → 168,783 today (174 files)** — +22k in the last week alone, while the debt campaign ran. Even exemplary PRs add machinery: #1281 (a Rust behavior fix) shipped +861 lines of new Python fence+twin; #1232 (CI debuggability) grew the giant pair by ~1,021 lines across a nine-round pinning arms race. The style, not the authors, is the engine.

What this diagnosis *keeps*: the invariants are right, the Rust core is fail-closed by construction, pin-the-blob is correct on adversarial surfaces, and sccache/fast-linker degrade-to-off is documented-legitimate. The problem is the default *style* — copies instead of single sources, hand-written twins instead of generated tests, enumeration instead of structure.

## Part 3 — Redesign plan (synthesis of #1016 + #1215 + #1275-17 + F2/F1)

**Target architecture — four pillars, success metric = removal:**

- **A. One fact, one home.** Every pinned expectation becomes a row in an importable table (extending the proven `ci_provenance.py` hub pattern). Verifier reads the table; the preflight test imports the same row; error strings derive from rule ids. A mergify value change becomes: edit `.mergify.yml` + one table row. One commit.
- **B. Kernel + rule engine** (#1215 WS1/WS2, #1016). One parsed model of the workflows; ~750–900 rules collapse into declarative rows (PIN/EQ/CROSS/FORBID/CLASSIFY evaluators); the ~9 genuinely custom checks stay hand-written. **Tests are generated from the table** — one mutation per rule, plus a falsifiability meta-test — retiring ~280 hand-written assertions. This kills the twin convention for everything tabular: a value change touches zero test files.
- **C. Sanctioned vocabularies** (#1275-17). Registry classification moves into code structure (literals live in their owning module, auto-exempted); `bolt-v3-runtime-literal-audit.toml` shrinks from 2,592 entries to true exceptions (target: dozens), context snippets dropped for symbol anchors.
- **D. One context seam + adjudicated fallbacks** (F2 front end, F1 as its fence). One declared "execution context" (CI / local / sandbox — what's required, what's optional-loud) replaces per-site env-tolerance; one TOML-loading seam replaces the three shadow parsers; the fallback census gets adjudicated with the survey's buckets (adjudicated-legit: sccache-style documented degrades; real-debt: silent auth-skip class; frontier: best-effort maintenance). The fence half (kernel symbols only defined in kernel files; new fallback shapes need a registry entry) is the enforcement of this behavior change, per the #1286/#1281 precedent — not a standalone validation layer.

**Migration sequence** (each tranche: golden findings-output captured per verifier before/after, differential tests shown to fail on pre-change code, revert-per-slice):

| Tranche | Content | Size (Codex sessions) |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Mergify family as the first rule-table tranche (kills the acute #1297 churn and proves pattern A+B together); fold F-N1 + pilot floors alongside | 1 |
| 1–5 | Remaining WS2 engine tranches by rule family; giant 16.5k→~5–6k, twin 19.1k→~4–5k, battery 195s→seconds (#1215 targets) | 5–6 |
| 6 | Kernel sweep (WS1: 9× stripper retirement, digest/schema unification, dead code) — parallel-safe with tranches 2+ | 2 |
| 7 | Shadow-parser consolidation per your D2 ruling + context seam + adjudicated fallback sweep of operational scripts | 2 |
| 8 | Vocabulary-registry migration (mechanically derivable from existing tags) | 2 |

Total ≈ **12–15 Codex sessions**. Already banked from #1215: P0/P1 speed and debuggability PRs (#1217/#1220/#1228/#1232/#1235/#1241 merged).

**Measured targets:** giant pair 35,639 → ~10k; registry 20,747 → hundreds; kernel dedup ~700–800; scripts/ net **−25k to −40k lines** with equal-or-stronger enforcement (migration manifest proves zero rules lost). **Churn acceptance test:** re-run the #1297 / #1151 / #1186 change classes — each must be a one-commit change touching config plus at most one table row, zero test edits; lockstep rate re-measured well below the current 86%.

**Collisions:** PRICE P1 (Rust) — disjoint, runs anytime. The pending micro-PR should shed its dual-TOML item (that's tranche 7's subject) and keep F-N1 + pilot floors — or fold both into tranche 0. Tranches 0–5 single-writer on the giant pair; tranche 6 parallel-safe; `verifier_io.py`, `justfile`, audit.toml remain single-writer hotspots.

**Your decision points:**
1. **D1 — Shadow parsers:** vendor one real parser everywhere, or drop old-Python support and fail loud (my recommendation: fail loud — it's your no-fallback rule applied to ourselves; the cargo shim still blocks, just with a clear message).
2. **D2 — Scope rule for latent breakage:** discovered-in-passing fixes go to their own micro-PR with an issue, never ride unrelated PRs (process rule; #1297 commit 2 is the exhibit).
3. **D3 — #1281's src/-wide Default allowlist:** re-scope to the owner module as part of tranche 0, or keep paying the tax (review already recommended re-scoping; you accepted the tax "for now").
4. **D4 — Tracking:** extend #1016/#1215 (already owner-endorsed, my recommendation) plus one new consolidated issue for the new scope (mirror single-sourcing, context seam/parsers, fallback sweep, registry split) — I'll file nothing without your per-target approval.
5. **D5 — Sequencing approval:** tranche 0 first, or start with the kernel sweep if you want lower-risk motion before touching the giant.

Stopping here as mandated — no issue filed, no code touched, PR #1297 left as-is (it's green; its parser growth becomes moot under D1). Approve, adjust, or challenge any piece.

content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme: `prefers-color-scheme` carries the OS preference, and the viewer's toggle stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, which must override the media query in both directions. The robust pattern is token-level: define the palette as custom properties on `:root`, redefine only the tokens under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` — style components through the tokens, never directly inside the media query — then redefine them again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` and `:root[data-theme="light"]`. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values — touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe — run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure — do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job — magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). → `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) — each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. → `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette — run the script, don't reason about ΔE.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,…>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory — or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, ≥8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. → `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer — by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. → `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For ≥ 2 series a legend is always present and ≤ 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box — the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** — its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout — open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** — it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue — it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale → two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake — see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light→dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD ≥ 12 is the
  target; 8–12 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view — it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for ≥ 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** — values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance — every value filled in — is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical — steps distinct from categorical |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

## Reference files

| File | What it answers |
|------|-----------------|
| `references/choosing-a-form.md` | Which chart type / is it even a chart? |
| `references/color-formula.md` | The four jobs, the six checks, snap-to-passing |
| `references/marks-and-anatomy.md` | Mark specs, spacers, labels, figures, hero number |
| `references/interaction.md` | Tooltips & hover, filters & time ranges |
| `references/components.md` | The pieces a chart is made of — build each in plain HTML |
| `references/anti-patterns.md` | **What goes wrong — check every chart against this** |
| `references/palette.md` | **The reference palette instance** — every parameter, filled in; swap for your brand's |
| `scripts/validate_palette.js` | Runnable six-checks validator (run it; don't eyeball) |

The problem, in one picture

I don't assess the success just by LoC, but what's the root cause and what can we do? is 10000 lines of code best?

No — 10,000 lines is not the goal, and you're right to push on it. Lines are just the gauge on the dashboard; here's the actual root cause and what "fixed" really means.

**The root cause, one level deeper than the copies.** This layer was built in ten weeks of incident response, fence by fence, by agents defending against agents. In that arms race, the only pattern that ever terminated a review round was maximum distrust: pin the exact bytes, so *any* change fails until every copy is updated. That posture is correct for the few surfaces where tampering is the real threat — merge-gate integrity, money invariants. But it got applied uniformly, to everything, including ordinary settings like batch sizes and retention days. A checker that pins bytes cannot tell **your intended change** from **an attack** — so every intended change pays the attack tax: someone must hand-update every copy before CI goes green. That's the machine that manufactures code. The copies, the twins, the 20k exceptions list are all downstream of one missing decision: *nobody ever classified which surfaces are hostile and which are cooperative.*

**So what does success actually look like?** Four tests, none of them line counts:

1. **No rule lost** — every one of the ~800 safety rules still fires (proven by before/after runs). That's the floor, not the win.
2. **An intended change costs one commit** — re-run the exact #1297 / #1151 / #1186 changes; each must be a single commit with zero hand-syncing. This is the direct measure of the root cause being gone.
3. **One home per fact** — no two implementations of the same fact or parser exist, so silent disagreement (the parser incident) becomes *impossible*, not just detected.
4. **The rules are readable** — a reviewer (or you) can see every rule as one line in a table, instead of archaeology through 16,000 lines.

**Why lines still show up in the plan:** when every remaining line is either a *rule decision* or a genuinely custom check — nothing a restatement of something else — the giant pair happens to land somewhere near 10k. If it lands at 12k or 8k, neither is better. LOC is how we'll *notice* we arrived, not where we're going.

**What we do differently given this framing:** the plan gains one explicit first step — classify every enforcement surface as *hostile* (keeps byte-pins: merge gate, money fences, execution-context checks) or *cooperative* (moves to property checks reading one source — "the gate depends on test-archive," not "these exact bytes exist"). That classification list comes to you for sign-off; it's the real design decision of the whole campaign. Session 1 stays the pilot.

Let me try again, much simpler.

**Your repo has safety alarms.** Their job is to catch anyone — especially a misbehaving AI — secretly changing important files.

**How the alarms work today: photocopies.** Each alarm keeps its own exact copy of what a file is *supposed* to say. If the real file ever differs from the photocopy — alarm goes off, CI turns red.

**Why they were built that way:** it's the only alarm a clever AI can't sneak past. Any difference at all gets caught. For the truly dangerous things — who can merge code, the money rules — this is exactly right.

**The problem:** a photocopy alarm can't tell a burglar from *you*. When you change a setting **on purpose** — like PR #1297's batch size — the alarm still goes off, and someone has to walk around updating every photocopy of that setting by hand before CI goes green. Some settings have four or five photocopies. That hand-updating is the mysterious "second commit" you keep seeing, and all those photocopies are most of the 168,000 lines.

**The mistake:** we used photocopy alarms for *everything* — harmless everyday settings included — not just the dangerous things.

**The fix:** sort everything into two piles, with your sign-off:
- **Dangerous pile** (merge rules, money rules): keep the photocopy alarms. They're doing their job.
- **Everyday pile** (batch sizes, timeouts, version numbers): throw away the photocopies. Write each setting in **one place only**, and make the checker *read* that place instead of remembering its own copy. Then changing a setting means changing it once — there's nothing left to go out of sync, so nothing to compensate.

**And "is 10,000 lines best?"** — lines don't matter by themselves. The test for each remaining line is: *is this a real decision, or a photocopy of something else?* Fixed = no photocopies left. The line count drops as a side effect of throwing them away, that's all.

Great question — and the honest answer is: no, photocopy alarms aren't the ideal even for the dangerous stuff. They're the *third-best* tool, and the repo has been reaching for them first. The optimal design is a hierarchy:

**1. Best: make the bad thing impossible, not detected.**
- **Money rules → the compiler.** #1281 already did this: invalid money values are now a *compile error*. No alarm needed — the bad code physically cannot build. The Python photocopy-allowlist layered on top is mostly redundant and should shrink, not grow.
- **Merge rules → GitHub's servers.** Branch protection, required checks, and your required reviewer live on GitHub's side. A malicious PR *cannot edit them*, so they need no photocopies at all. This already exists in your repo — it's the real merge authority.

**2. Second: one small guard booth instead of alarms on every window.**
Whatever must still be checked in-repo goes into one small kernel — target a couple thousand lines, not 168,000 — that CI runs **from the main branch's copy**, so a PR can't tamper with the guard that's judging it (the gate already uses this trick). Changes to the kernel and governance files require your review by path rule (server-enforced, zero lines of code). The kernel checks *properties* read from single sources.

**3. Last resort: photocopies.**
Only for the handful of spots the first two genuinely can't reach — each one with a written reason.

**Why this is the real optimum:** every security design ends at something you simply have to trust. Today that "something" is 168,000 lines nobody — including you — can actually read. The optimal design shrinks what-must-be-trusted down to three things a human can genuinely verify: **GitHub's settings page, the Rust compiler, and one small kernel you can read in an afternoon.** The photocopy explosion happened because agents kept compensating for the fact that no one could review everything — the fix is to make the thing that needs reviewing small, not to add more alarms.

+# Investigation Report: Deeply Nested Conditionals and Fallback Patterns
+
+## 1. Executive Summary
+
+This report analyzes two major technical debt patterns in the `bolt-v2` codebase:
+1.  **Fallback Patterns:** Extensive use of `unwrap_or`, `unwrap_or_default`, and empty `else` blocks instead of explicit error handling.
+2.  **Monolithic & Deeply Nested Code:** Extremely long functions with `if` conditionals stacked up to 6+ levels deep (24+ spaces of indentation).
+
+These patterns are primarily found in massive files such as `src/strategies/binary_oracle_edge_taker/mod.rs` (8,200+ lines) and `src/bolt_v3_submit_admission.rs` (4,400+ lines).
+
+As noted by senior engineers, while AI agents (and junior developers) prioritize "making it work" quickly, relying on fallbacks masks underlying errors, making the system fragile, hard to debug, and prone to failing silently.
+
+## 2. Root Cause Analysis
+
+### Fallback Patterns
+- **Why they emerge:** Developers and AI agents use `unwrap_or(default_value)` to bypass Rust's strict error handling and get code compiling rapidly.
+- **The problem:** If a critical value (e.g., a reference price, a configuration value, or a health status) is missing, substituting a silent default allows the program to continue with invalid state. This leads to subtle downstream bugs (e.g., incorrect pricing or admission decisions) that are notoriously hard to trace back to their source.
+- **Examples Found:**
+  - Over 110 instances of `unwrap_or` in non-test files.
+  - In `src/strategies/binary_oracle_edge_taker/mod.rs` (lines 1813-1866), `unwrap_or` is used to silently default the `ReferencePriceSourceStatus` to `Silent` if health information is missing.
+  - In `src/bolt_v3_submit_admission.rs` (lines 1141, 1685), critical liability tracking and admission rejection reasons fallback to `Decimal::ZERO` and `Rejected` instead of explicitly handling the absent state.
+
+### Monolithic and Deeply Nested Code
+- **Why they emerge:** Incremental additions of new business logic, edge cases, and safety checks over time without periodic refactoring.
+- **The problem:** Deeply nested code (the "Arrow Anti-Pattern") increases cognitive load, hides the main execution path, and makes unit testing specific branches difficult.
+- **Examples Found:**
+  - `src/strategies/binary_oracle_edge_taker/mod.rs` contains conditionals nested up to 7 levels deep (e.g., line 1790: `if reference_quote_outside_live_window(...)`, line 7165: `if resized_executable_edge.trade_allowed && resized_notional_supported`).
+
+## 3. Concrete Refactoring Strategy
+
+To align with senior engineering standards and eliminate these anti-patterns, the following strategies should be applied incrementally to avoid system instability.
+
+### Strategy 1: Eliminate Silent Fallbacks (Fail Loudly)
+- **Action:** Replace `unwrap_or` and `unwrap_or_default` with explicit error handling.
+- **How:**
+  - If a missing value indicates a fatal system state or invalid configuration, use `expect("descriptive message")` or `panic!()` to fail fast.
+  - If the absence is an expected runtime state, propagate the error using `Result` and the `?` operator.
+  - If a fallback is genuinely required by business logic, document *why* the fallback is mathematically or logically sound, rather than just returning `0` or `false`.
+
+### Strategy 2: Flatten Nested Conditionals (Guard Clauses)
+- **Action:** Refactor deeply nested `if` statements using guard clauses and early returns.
+- **How:** Reverse the conditional logic to exit the function early if preconditions are not met. This keeps the "happy path" un-nested at the bottom of the function.
+  *Before:*
+  ```rust
+  if condition_a {
+      if condition_b {
+          // do work
+      }
+  }
+  ```
+  *After:*
+  ```rust
+  if !condition_a { return; }
+  if !condition_b { return; }
+  // do work
+  ```
+
+### Strategy 3: Break Down Monoliths
+- **Action:** Extract complex, nested logic blocks into well-named, independent helper functions or separate modules.
+- **How:** In `binary_oracle_edge_taker/mod.rs`, isolate pricing logic, state evaluation, and risk checks into separate files (e.g., `pricing.rs`, `risk.rs`). In `bolt_v3_submit_admission.rs`, extract the core evaluation loops.
+
+## 4. Conclusion and Next Steps
+
+The presence of these patterns degrades maintainability and system safety. By adopting a strict "fail loudly" philosophy and enforcing flat, modular code structures, the codebase will become more robust and easier to extend.
+
+**Recommended Next Step:** Create targeted, single-responsibility PRs to refactor the specific fallback occurrences identified in `bolt_v3_submit_admission.rs`, replacing them with explicit `match` statements and error propagation.

Verdict: **not valid as an actionable finding — recommend closing without merge.** Its numbers are honest, its three concrete examples are all wrong, and its recommended next step re-proposes a change that was already tried and closed as dangerous.

The three examples, against the actual code:

1. **Edge-taker "silently defaults health to Silent"** — the code defaults missing health to **`Stale`** (the report even misnames the variant), and `Stale` *blocks* trading via the staleness gate. That's the conservative direction — the opposite of masking.
2. **`submit_admission:1141` "liability falls back to Decimal::ZERO"** — that line sits inside building a **rejection record** (the order is already being refused for missing evidence). Good question to push on — checking just changed my answer. The installer **copies** the shim as a single standalone file onto your PATH (`install-cargo-shim:104`), so a parser vendored in the repo would *not* travel with it. Plain "vendor one parser everywhere" doesn't work for the shim without adding install-time bundling machinery — which would be new machinery, exactly what we're not doing.

So the best solution is a hybrid, and it's cleaner than my original recommendation:

1. **The shim keeps one tiny reader — but fenced.** It only ever needs two things from the policy file, its section-scoping bug (finding #2) gets fixed, and a CI parity test asserts the shim's reader and the real parser agree on the actual policy file. That converts the failure mode we saw last week (silent breakage on Macs, discovered days later inside an unrelated PR) into a loud CI failure *on the PR that introduces the incompatible syntax*. The divergence class becomes structurally impossible to miss.
2. **The other two scripts lose their hand-rolled parsers entirely.** They live in the repo where sharing is free: one shared reading seam — real parser when available, and the single shared minimal reader (the same code the shim uses, kept in one file) below Python 3.11.

Net effect: three divergent home-made parsers become **one small one, in one place, with a fence that proves it agrees with the real parser on every commit**. No third-party code checked in, no install machinery, and the "same file must parse identically under any Python" contract becomes enforced instead of hoped.

Two answers — one about `if` in general, one about a real flaw your eye just caught again.

**Why checker code is full of `if`:** there are three kinds, and only one is the enemy.
1. *"What kind of thing is this?"* — deciding how to walk a dict vs a list. Fine.
2. *"Is this wrong? Then complain."* — that's the entire job of a checker; a fence is literally made of these.
3. *"It's missing — quietly use something else and keep going."* — the banned one.
The diff you pasted is kinds 1 and 2. A checker with zero conditionals can't check anything. Your ban was never "no `if`" — it's "no `if` that hides a problem."

**But your instinct flagged something genuinely wrong here:** those registered payloads pinned to **line numbers** — `("verify_ci_workflow_hygiene.py", 10128)`. That's the exact disease we're eliminating: in a 16,000-line file, any edit above line 10128 shifts it, the fence breaks, someone rubber-stamps a new number — the churn machine reborn inside the tool meant to kill it. And look at *what's* being registered: `"]"` — a single closing bracket. If the fence thinks a lone `]` is a "protected config value," the protected set is too crude, and no amount of registration fixes that; the fix is to not protect syntax fragments in the first place.

Send this to the **Job B session**:

> Correction to the retype-fence: (1) Remove line-number-scoped registered payloads entirely — (file, line) pins break on any edit above them; this repo anchors on symbols, never line numbers. (2) The root cause is over-protection: the protected-string set must exclude trivial/syntax-only fragments — apply a content rule (e.g., strip the line; protect only if it contains a key=value, a name, or ≥ some minimal information content; a lone bracket, comma, or quote is never protected). With that rule, the `"]"` registrations disappear instead of being catalogued at nine line addresses. (3) Any registration that legitimately remains is scoped by file path or enclosing symbol, with a reason — never by line number. Add a test arm proving a syntax-only line is not protected and a real value line still is.

The pattern for you to keep: every time you've asked "why is this conditional here," it's been worth asking. Kind 1 and 2 answers mean it's fine; the moment the answer involves line numbers or "quietly skip," you've found the disease.

Your instinct is measured fact, not impression — it **is** worsening: the main strategy file was cut to 5,972 lines two weeks ago and has already regrown to 8,272 (+2,300 in five days), and the checker layer grew 22,000 lines in a week. So before "how to split big files," the more important answer is **why they regrow: new work keeps landing *into* the big files**, because they're the default landing zone — every new feature goes into `mod.rs`, every new CI rule into the giant checker. Splitting without changing the landing zone is mowing a lawn that's being fertilized.

So the best way to refactor these, in order:

1. **Change where new code lands (the actual fix).** For the checker layer, that's exactly Job B: new rules become *table rows*, not code in the giant — after conversion, the giant physically can't regrow. are you 100% confident about this

No — and you should distrust anyone who says 100% here. My honest breakdown:

- **The facts: near-100%.** Everything measured — the copies, the growth numbers, the Mergify bypass, the adapter's 532-row tax — was verified by command, most of it twice (me plus a hostile reviewer).
- **The verdicts: high, not total.** Judgments like "this family never caught anything" can be wrong — the adversary itself pointed out that squash-merging erases the evidence of past catches. Some "delete" rows could be mistaken.
- **The design: doesn't need me to be right.** That's the actual answer. The plan assumes I'm fallible: nothing guarding money, merges, or secrets can be deleted at all; every other deletion happens only after a live probe shows what really blocks what; each family is deleted in its own PR, reversible with one command; and the process just demonstrated — twice — that it catches its own authors' errors, including mine.

So the confidence that matters isn't "Claude is sure." It's: **the worst realistic mistake is one deleted family that turns out to matter, which is detected by a loud failure and restored in one command.** That's a bounded, recoverable downside — versus the measured, compounding cost of keeping things as they are.

That's as honest as I can make it. If any single row worries you, name it and it moves to "keep until proven useless" — that costs almost nothing.

Net effect of your two points: the plan now attacks the debt at both ends — deleting the checking layer that grew around the code, and deleting the code that grew around NT.

**And now it freezes.** The amended verdict table is the plan of record. From this point, no change happens because anyone — including me — has a better idea. A change requires a **failed probe**: execution evidence that a verdict was wrong. Ideas are done; only results can amend the plan now.

so why did you suggest 1305, and why are we closing 1305 now?

Fair question — here's the honest accounting.

**Why I suggested it:** at the time, I was operating under one constraint — *every one of the ~800 existing checks must survive* (my over-strict reading of your "never drop a safety gate" rule). Under that constraint, deletion was off the table, so the only way to kill the photocopy problem was to *convert* all the checks into a rule-table engine. #1305 was step one of that conversion: build the engine, prove it on the smallest family.

**Why we're closing it:** the constraint itself turned out to be wrong, and the evidence killed it twice over:

1. **The conversion was a bad trade, measured:** #1305 added a net +2,223 lines to convert just 30 checks — the cure was growing the disease. And the engine drifted three times *while being built*, proving conversion doesn't escape the agent-drift problem either.
2. **The policy changed underneath it:** the adversarial review established that most of the 800 checks pin *shape*, not safety — so the default flipped from "convert everything" to "delete what can't justify itself." An engine built to host 800 rules has no purpose when most of those rules are dying and the few survivors are being kept as-is or becoming schemas.

So #1305 isn't being closed because the work was sloppy — it's being closed because **the requirement it was built to serve was cancelled.** Keeping it would mean landing 2,200 lines of scaffolding for a building we decided not to construct.

What that session actually bought, so it's not written off as pure waste: it proved empirically that even purpose-built machinery drifts (which drove the whole approach reset), and it mapped exactly which code depends on the mergify checks — knowledge the adversary then used to correct the deletion plan.

That's the pattern behind the back-and-forth feeling in one sentence: **the suggestion was right under the old assumption; the assumption was disproven; keeping the suggestion after its assumption died would be the actual mistake.**
so what can we do about the overall work? I'm asking not in the context of 1305 but overall work

Here's what the last two days actually taught us about how to run **all** the work — codified as the operating model from now on:

1. **Nothing starts from an idea — everything starts from a measured fact.** "Adapters were hard" became a real work item only after we measured *532 registry rows for one venue*. Any proposed work that can't point to its number doesn't start.
2. **Plans get attacked before they get executed.** Both adversarial reviews caught errors — including mine — for the cost of minutes. That's now a standing gate: no multi-session plan runs until a second Fable has tried to break it.
3. **The default action is delete, not add.** Any PR that grows the codebase has to justify itself; shrinking ones don't. This inverts the incentive that created the mess.
4. **Agents don't write open-ended code anymore.** Their work is scoped to deletions, moves, and filling in data — the forms where the disease can't be written. New logic is the rare exception and gets the heaviest review.
5. **Every job ships with a test *you* can verify without reading code.** "Change that value again — is it one commit?" "Add a venue — how many files?" If the acceptance test needs a programmer, it's the wrong test.
6. **Steps stay small and reversible.** One family per PR, one command to undo. Being wrong is allowed; being expensively wrong is not.
7. **Your role is exactly two things: name the pain, and make policy calls.** You never review code, and you never should have — every catch you made this week is now a machine's job or an adversary's job.
8. **Plans freeze after the gate.** Changes require a failed probe — evidence — never a better idea. That ends the back-and-forth for good.

That's the answer for the overall work: not a new plan, but a way of working under which the failures you kept seeing — drift, hardcodes, wasted sessions, you as the last line of defense — structurally can't recur.

Saving this as the standing operating model now; the frozen next actions (probe the merge gate, merge #1304, close #1305) execute under it.

Three questions, three straight answers:

**Why these two first?**
- The **probe** is first because the frozen rule is *measure before delete* — every deletion PR that follows has to cite what the probe showed actually blocks a hostile merge. Doing it first means no later step ever waits on it, and it costs one throwaway PR.
- The **extraction** is first because it gates the single biggest removal. The giant pair can't be deleted while the 9 real detectors and the merge guard live *inside* it — and there's a built-in waiting period: CI runs the *previous* version of these checks against each PR, so the old entry points must stay alive for one merge cycle after extraction. That forced wait is exactly why extraction starts now: the clock runs while everything else proceeds.

**Why are we sure this removes the tech debt?**
"Sure" isn't the claim — *measured* is. The debt was never a feeling; it was numbers: the giant pair is 21% of the layer, the registry is 20,747 lines (532 of its rows are one adapter's tax), the twins are 55%, and 86% of changes paid a copy-tax. Each step removes one of those measured components, and each has a test you can run yourself without reading code — the one-commit change test (already passed once, after #1301) and, at the end, the adapter-footprint test. What stops the debt from *growing back* is already live as of yesterday's merges: the fallback fence with its ratchet, and the operating model where agents fill tables and delete rather than write open code. Honest residual: a deletion could hit something silently load-bearing — bounded by probe-first, one-family-per-PR, one-command revert, and money/merge/secrets being untouchable.

**Is this the long pole?**
Yes — the giant-pair sequence (extract → wait one merge cycle → delete → convert survivors to schemas) sets the campaign's calendar, precisely because of that mandatory waiting period and because only one session at a time may touch those files. The registry burn-down is the other big mass, but it's parallel-safe (different files, mostly mechanical), so it hides inside the giant's timeline. That chain is longer than the giant sequence and it's what actually converts this cleanup into business capability. It starts right after the registry work, which runs in parallel with the giant anyway.

The probe did its job, and the result is decisive — plus it surfaced a security fact you should know.

**What it proved (verified myself):** a pull request *can* publish its own check named `gate` and mark it successful, and — the part that matters — it's **indistinguishable from the real one**, because both are published by the same GitHub Actions app. The only reason the hostile PR stayed blocked is that the *real* gate also ran, failed, and its failure won among the two same-named checks — plus your review was still missing.

**What that means for the plan — decisive:** the merge-gate checks (`verify_mergify_config`, the gate-naming logic, the tamper pins) are **not deletable and cannot move to GitHub.** GitHub's own protection is bypassed by Mergify *and* can't tell a fake gate from a real one — so your local checks plus your review are the actual lock. This is the "measure before delete" rule paying for itself: my original plan was to move gate protection to GitHub and delete the local copies — the probe proves that would have **removed the only real enforcement and opened a bypass.** The adversary's amendment to keep them is now measured-true, not just argued. No verdict changes; the keepers are confirmed keepers with evidence.

**One separate finding, worth flagging (not a tech-debt item, and I won't act on it without you):** the system holds only *because* the real gate runs and fails. If a PR could ever make the real gate skip while posting a fake success, Mergify's `check-success = gate` could in principle be satisfied. This is a pre-existing, narrow merge-security exposure — not created by any of this work. If you want, I can open one issue documenting it for later; otherwise I leave it recorded in memory.
